title: Obtaining Post-Skinning Vertices from GPU Skin Cache
abstract: How to consume animated skeletal positions after compute skinning without reading them back to the CPU—and how to reason about scheduling, buffer lifetime, tangents, and motion history.
imageAlt: Compute skinning writes animated vertices that subdivision and draw passes consume on the GPU
cardImageAlt: Project material diagram of GPU skinning output feeding OpenSubdiv refinement buffers
lede: If a compute shader needs the final animated surface, the useful answer is not a CPU readback. It is to consume the same GPU Skin Cache output that Unreal already produces for later rendering work. The hard parts are ordering and ownership, not the stencil arithmetic that comes afterward.

sections.heading: What ‘post-skinning’ means
paragraphs: Source skeletal vertices are stored in a reference pose with bone indices and weights. Skinning transforms each source position and direction by a weighted combination of the current bone transforms. The resulting stream is instance-specific and changes with the pose.

In the traditional path that computation happens inside the vertex shader, so there may be no reusable buffer containing every final vertex. The GPU Skin Cache changes the architecture: a compute pass skins the mesh into cached GPU buffers, and later passes read those results through a pass-through vertex factory.

sections.heading: The zero-readback strategy
paragraphs: Enable compute skinning for the target platform and material configuration, let the Skin Cache allocate and write its position stream, then schedule the custom compute work after that write. Bind the cached stream as a shader resource and write subdivision output into a separate unordered-access buffer. Finally, make the draw’s vertex factory consume the refined stream.

This keeps animation, refinement, and rendering on the GPU. A readback would add synchronization, latency, bandwidth, and a second upload before the data could be drawn again. It is useful for debugging a handful of values, not as the production data path.

sections.heading: Synchronization is part of correctness
paragraphs: A pointer to a GPU buffer is not proof that its current-frame contents are ready. The custom pass must be ordered after Skin Cache writes and before any draw that consumes refinement output. It also needs correct resource-state transitions between unordered access, shader-resource access, and vertex-buffer access.

In a render-graph implementation, express these dependencies as pass inputs and outputs so the graph can place transitions and retain resources. In older manual command-list code, the same dependencies still exist; they are merely easier to omit. Never rely on the fact that two commands happened to execute in the desired order in one capture.

sections.heading: Position alone is not a renderable surface
paragraphs: A convincing prototype can stop at positions; a production path cannot. Lighting needs normals and tangents, textured materials need UVs, motion blur needs previous positions, and ray tracing or distance fields may need separate updates. Decide whether each attribute is stencil-evaluated, recomputed from refined triangles, preserved as face-varying data, or intentionally unsupported.

Motion history deserves special attention. If the current frame is refined from current skinned positions, velocity requires the equivalent previous-frame refined position—or a consistent way to reconstruct it. Mixing a refined current stream with an unrefined previous stream produces false motion.

sections.heading: A focused validation sequence
paragraphs: First render cached positions as points or a flat unlit mesh and compare a frozen pose with the normal Skin Cache draw. Then animate one bone and verify that the refined output changes in the same frame. Next inspect two consecutive frames and validate motion vectors. Only after these tests should materials, shadows, and multiple LODs be added.

Measure the GPU result without stalling the CPU. Timestamp the skinning and refinement passes, inspect barriers in a frame capture, and verify that the output allocation is reused rather than recreated each frame. A correct result with an accidental readback or per-frame resource churn is not a finished GPU path.

numberedSteps.title: No readback

numberedSteps.title: Stable allocation
numberedSteps.text: Buffers are pooled or retained; they are not recreated for every pose.

callouts.title: Do not keep transient internals forever
callouts.text: Skin Cache implementation details can change across engine versions. Encapsulate access behind a small engine integration point and revalidate it when upgrading.

sections.heading: Exit criteria for the GPU path
paragraphs: The path is usable when current and previous refined streams are produced on the GPU, downstream passes consume the intended attributes, resource transitions are visible in a frame capture, and animation produces no CPU readback or per-frame allocation churn. A correct bind-pose screenshot meets only the first debugging milestone.
bullets: Current pose and previous pose are both defined.
Position, tangent basis, UVs, and section identity have explicit owners.
Skin Cache → refine → draw order is expressed as a dependency.
Base, depth, shadow, and velocity passes have been checked.

closing: Required contract: read the current Skin Cache stream after its producer pass, write a separate refined stream, and bind that stream consistently in every required consumer pass.
